entries.d7b3ea56757690beefd2fc7c62a8234be370d374: <div sID="gen8131" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="13" osisID="2Chr.13" sID="2Chr.13"/> <div eID="gen8131" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8132" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen8133" type="x-p"/> We have here a much fuller account of the reign of Abijah, the son of Rehoboam, than we had in the Kings. There we found that his character was no better than his father's—he "walked in the sins of his father, and his heart was not right with God," <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.2-1Kgs.15.3">1 Kings xv. 2, 3</reference>. But here we find him more brave and successful in war than his father was. He reigned but three years, and was chiefly famous for a glorious victory he obtained over the forces of Jeroboam. Here we have, I. The armies brought into the field on both sides, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">ver. 3</reference>. The remonstrance which Abijah made before the battle, setting forth the justice of his cause, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.4-2Chr.13.12">ver. 4-12</reference>. III. The distress which Judah was brought into by the policy of Jeroboam, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.13-2Chr.13.14">ver. 13, 14</reference>. IV. The victory they obtained notwithstanding, by the power of God, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.15-2Chr.13.20">ver. 15-20</reference>. V. The conclusion of Abijah's reign, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.21-2Chr.13.22">ver. 21, 22</reference>.
entries.e0292ca0553031d04668bd4679b6fc916180c40d: <div eID="gen8133" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen8132" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Abijah's Reign over Judah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 957.)</title> <div sID="gen8134" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Now in the eighteenth year of king Jeroboam began Abijah to reign over Judah. <hi type="super">2</hi> He reigned three years in Jerusalem. His mother's name also <hi type="italic">was</hi> Michaiah the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah. And there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam. <hi type="super">3</hi> And Abijah set the battle in array with an army of valiant men of war, <hi type="italic">even</hi> four hundred thousand chosen men: Jeroboam also set the battle in array against him with eight hundred thousand chosen men, <hi type="italic">being</hi> mighty men of valour. <hi type="super">4</hi> And Abijah stood up upon mount Zemaraim, which <hi type="italic">is</hi> in mount Ephraim, and said, Hear me, thou Jeroboam, and all Israel; <hi type="super">5</hi> Ought ye not to know that the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of Israel gave the kingdom over Israel to David for ever, <hi type="italic">even</hi> to him and to his sons by a covenant of salt? <hi type="super">6</hi> Yet Jeroboam the son of Nebat, the servant of Solomon the son of David, is risen up, and hath rebelled against his lord. <hi type="super">7</hi> And there are gathered unto him vain men, the children of Belial, and have strengthened themselves against Rehoboam the son of Solomon, when Rehoboam was young and tenderhearted, and could not withstand them. <hi type="super">8</hi> And now ye think to withstand the kingdom of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> in the hand of the sons of David; and ye <hi type="italic">be</hi> a great multitude, and <hi type="italic">there are</hi> with you golden calves, which Jeroboam made you for gods. <hi type="super">9</hi> Have ye not cast out the priests of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , the sons of Aaron, and the Levites, and have made you priests after the manner of the nations of <hi type="italic">other</hi> lands? so that whosoever cometh to consecrate himself with a young bullock and seven rams, <hi type="italic">the same</hi> may be a priest of <hi type="italic">them that are</hi> no gods. <hi type="super">10</hi> But as for us, the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> <hi type="italic">is</hi> our God, and we have not forsaken him; and the priests, which minister unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , <hi type="italic">are</hi> the sons of Aaron, and the Levites <hi type="italic">wait</hi> upon <hi type="italic">their</hi> business: <hi type="super">11</hi> And they burn unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> every morning and every evening burnt sacrifices and sweet incense: the showbread also <hi type="italic">set they in order</hi> upon the pure table; and the candlestick of gold with the lamps thereof, to burn every evening: for we keep the charge of the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> our God; but ye have forsaken him. <hi type="super">12</hi> And, behold, God himself <hi type="italic">is</hi> with us for <hi type="italic">our</hi> captain, and his priests with sounding trumpets to cry alarm against you. O children of Israel, fight ye not against the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of your fathers; for ye shall not prosper. <div eID="gen8134" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> Abijah's mother was called <hi type="italic">Maachah,</hi> the daughter of Absalom, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20">ch. xi. 20</reference>; here she is called <hi type="italic">Michaiah,</hi> the daughter of Uriel. It is most probable that she was a grand-daughter of Absalom, by his daughter Tamar (<reference osisRef="2Sam.14.27">2 Sam. xiv. 27</reference>), and that her immediate father was this Uriel. But we are here to attend Abijah into the field of battle with Jeroboam king of Israel. <div eID="gen8135" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8136" type="x-p"/> I. God gave him leave to engage with Jeroboam, and owned him in the conflict, though he would not permit Rehoboam to do it, <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.4">ch. xi. 4</reference>. 1. Jeroboam, it is probable, was now the aggressor, and what Abijah did was in his own necessary defence. Jeroboam, it may be, happening to survive Rehoboam, claimed the crown of Judah be survivorship, at least hoped to get it from this young king, upon his accession to the throne. Against these impudent pretensions it was brave in Abijah to take up arms, and God stood by him. 2. When Rehoboam attempted to recover his ten tribes Jeroboam was upon his good behaviour, and there must be some trial of him; but now that he had discovered what manner of man he was, by setting up the calves and casting off the priests, Abijah is allowed to chastise him, and it does not appear that he intended any more; whereas Rehoboam aimed at no less than the utter reduction of the ten tribes, which was contrary to the counsel of God. <div eID="gen8136" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8137" type="x-p"/> II. Jeroboam's army was double in number to that of Abijah (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">v. 3</reference>), for he had ten tribes to raise an army out of, while Abijah had but two. Of the army on both sides it is said, they were <hi type="italic">mighty men, chosen men,</hi> and <hi type="italic">valiant;</hi> but the army of Judah consisted only of 400,000, while Jeroboam's army amounted to 800 000. The inferior number however proved victorious; for the battle is not always to the strong nor the cause to the majority. <div eID="gen8137" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8138" type="x-p"/> III. Abijah, before he fought them, reasoned with them, to persuade them, though not to return to the house of David (that matter was settled by the divine determination and he acquiesced), yet to desist from fighting against the house of David. He would not have them <hi type="italic">withstand the kingdom of the Lord in the hands of the sons of David</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.8">v. 8</reference>), but at least to be content with what they had. Note, It is good to try reason before we use force. If the point may be gained by dint of argument, better so than by dint of sword. We must never fly to violent methods till all the arts of persuasion have been tried in vain. War must be the <hi type="italic">ultima ratio regum</hi>—<hi type="italic">the last resort of kings.</hi> Fair reasoning may do a great deal of good and prevent a good deal of mischief. <hi type="italic">How forcible are right words!</hi> Abijah had got with his army into the heart of their country; for he made this speech upon a hill in Mount Ephraim, where he might be heard by Jeroboam and the principal officers, with whom it is probable he desired to have a treaty, to which they consented. It has been usual for great generals to make speeches to their soldiers to animate them, and this speech of Abijah had some tendency to do this, but was directed to Jeroboam and all Israel. Two things Abijah undertakes to make out, for the satisfaction of his own men and the conviction of the enemy:— <div eID="gen8138" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8139" type="x-p"/> 1. That he had right on his side, a <hi type="italic">jus divinum</hi>—<hi type="italic">a divine right:</hi> "You know, or ought to know, that <hi type="italic">God gave the kingdom to David and his sons for ever</hi>" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.5">v. 5</reference>), not by common providence, his usual way of disposing of kingdoms, but by a covenant of salt, a lasting covenant, a covenant made by sacrifice, which was always salted; so bishop Patrick. All Israel had owned that David was a king of God's making, and that God had entailed the crown upon his family; so that Jeroboam's taking the crown of Israel at first was not justifiable: yet it is not certain that Abijah referred chiefly to that, for he knew that Jeroboam had a grant from God of the ten tribes. His attempt, however, to disturb the peace and possession of the king of Judah was by no means excusable; for when the ten tribes were given to him two were reserved for the house of David. Abijah shows, (1.) That there was a great deal of dishonesty and disingenuousness in Jeroboam's first setting himself up: He <hi type="italic">rebelled against his lord</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.6">v. 6</reference>) who had preferred him (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.28">1 Kings xi. 28</reference>), and basely took advantage of Rehoboam's weakness in a critical juncture, when, in gratitude to his old master and in justice to his title, he ought rather to have stood by him, and helped to secure the people in their allegiance to him, than to head a party against him and make a prey of him, which was unworthily done and what he could not expect to prosper in. Those that supported him are here called <hi type="italic">vain men</hi> (a character perhaps borrowed from <reference osisRef="Judg.11.3">Judg. xi. 3</reference>), men that did not act from any steady principle, but were given to change, and men of Belial, that were for shaking off the yoke of government and setting those over them that would do just as they would have them do. (2.) That there was a great deal of impiety in his present attempt; for, in fighting against the house of David, he fought <hi type="italic">against the kingdom of the Lord.</hi> Those who oppose right oppose the righteous God who sits in the throne judging right, and cannot promise themselves success in so doing. Right may indeed go by the worst for a time, but it will prevail at last. <div eID="gen8139" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8140" type="x-p"/> 2. That he had God on his side. This he insisted much upon, that the religion of Jeroboam and his army was false and idolatrous, but that he and his people, the men of Judah, had the pure worship of the true and living God among them. It appears from the character given of Abijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.3">1 Kings xv. 3</reference>) that he was not himself in this war chiefly from the religion of his kingdom. For, (1.) Whatever he was otherwise, it should seem that he was no idolator, or, if he connived at the high places and images (<reference osisRef="2Chr.14.3">ch. xiv. 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.5">5</reference>), yet he constantly kept up the temple-service. (2.) Whatever corruptions there were in the kingdom of Judah, the state of religion among them was better than in the kingdom of Israel, with which they were now contending. (3.) It is common for those that deny the power of godliness to boast of the form of it. (4.) It was the cause of his kingdom that he was pleading; and, though he was not himself so good as he should have been, yet he hoped that, for the sake of the good men and good things that were in Judah, God would now appear for them. Many that have little religion themselves yet have so much sense and grace as to value it in others. See how he describes, [1.] The apostasy of Israel from God. "<hi type="italic">You are a great multitude,</hi>" said he, "far superior to us in number; but we need not fear you, for you have that among yourselves which is enough to ruin you. For," <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "You have calves for your gods (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.8">v. 8</reference>), that are unable to protect and help you and will certainly cause the true and living God to oppose you. Those will be Achans, troublers of your camp." <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> "You have base men for your priests, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.9">v. 9</reference>. You have cast off the tribes of Levi, and the house of Aaron, whom God appointed to minister in holy things; and, in conformity to the custom of the idolatrous nations, make any man a priest that has a mind to the office and will be at the charge of the consecration, though ever so much a scandal to the office." Yet such, though very unfit to be priests, were fittest of all to be <hi type="italic">their</hi> priests; for what more agreeable to gods that were no gods than priests that were no priests? Like to like, both pretenders and usurpers. [2.] The adherence of Judah to God: "<hi type="italic">But as for us</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.10">v. 10</reference>) <hi type="italic">we have not forsaken God.</hi> Jehovah is our God, the God of our fathers, the God of Israel, who is able to protect us, and give us success. He is with us, for we are with him." <hi type="italic">First,</hi> "At home in his temple: We <hi type="italic">keep his charge,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.10-2Chr.13.11">v. 10, 11</reference>. We worship no images, have no priests but what he has ordained, no rites of worship but what he has prescribed. Both the temple service and the temple furniture are of his appointing. His appointment we abide by, and neither add nor diminish. These we have the comfort of, these we now stand up in the defence of: so that upon a religious as well as a civil account we have the better cause. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Here in the camp; he is our captain, and we may therefore be sure that he is with us, because we are with him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.12">v. 12</reference>. And, as a token of his presence, we have here with us his priests, sounding his trumpets according to the law, as a testimony against you, and an assurance to us that in the day of battle we shall be <hi type="italic">remembered before the Lord our God</hi> and <hi type="italic">saved from our enemies;</hi>" for so this sacred signal is explained, <reference osisRef="Num.10.9">Num. x. 9</reference>. Nothing is more effectual to embolden men, and put spirit into them, than to be sure that God is with them and fights for them. He concludes with fair warning to his enemies. "<hi type="italic">Fight not against the God of your fathers.</hi> It is folly to fight against the God of almighty power; but it is treachery and base ingratitude to fight against your fathers' God, and you cannot expect to prosper."
entries.76fd82d57d61714b199d0675bd8faf2a3d9fc311: <div eID="gen8140" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Jeroboam Defeated by Abijah. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 957.)</title> <div sID="gen8141" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">13</hi> But Jeroboam caused an ambushment to come about behind them: so they were before Judah, and the ambushment <hi type="italic">was</hi> behind them. <hi type="super">14</hi> And when Judah looked back, behold, the battle <hi type="italic">was</hi> before and behind: and they cried unto the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> , and the priests sounded with the trumpets. <hi type="super">15</hi> Then the men of Judah gave a shout: and as the men of Judah shouted, it came to pass, that God smote Jeroboam and all Israel before Abijah and Judah. <hi type="super">16</hi> And the children of Israel fled before Judah: and God delivered them into their hand. <hi type="super">17</hi> And Abijah and his people slew them with a great slaughter: so there fell down slain of Israel five hundred thousand chosen men. <hi type="super">18</hi> Thus the children of Israel were brought under at that time, and the children of Judah prevailed, because they relied upon the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> God of their fathers. <hi type="super">19</hi> And Abijah pursued after Jeroboam, and took cities from him, Beth-el with the towns thereof, and Jeshanah with the towns thereof, and Ephrain with the towns thereof. <hi type="super">20</hi> Neither did Jeroboam recover strength again in the days of Abijah: and the <hi type="small-caps">Lord</hi> struck him, and he died. <hi type="super">21</hi> But Abijah waxed mighty, and married fourteen wives, and begat twenty and two sons, and sixteen daughters. <hi type="super">22</hi> And the rest of the acts of Abijah, and his ways, and his sayings, <hi type="italic">are</hi> written in the story of the prophet Iddo. <div eID="gen8141" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8142" type="x-p"/> We do not find that Jeroboam offered to make any answer at all to Abijah's speech. Though it was much to the purpose, he resolved not to heed it, and therefore he heard it as though he heard it not. He came to fight, not to dispute. The longest sword, he thought, would determine the matter, not the better cause. Let us therefore see the issue, whether right and religion carried the day or no. <div eID="gen8142" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8143" type="x-p"/> I. Jeroboam, who trusted to his politics, was beaten. He was so far from fair reasoning that he was not for fair fighting. We may suppose that he felt a sovereign contempt for Abijah's harangue. "One stratagem," thinks he, "is worth twenty such speeches; we will soon give him an answer to all his arguments; he shall soon find himself overpowered with numbers, surrounded on every side with the instruments of death, and then let him boast of his religion and his title to the crown." A parley, it is probable, was agreed on, yet Jeroboam basely takes the advantage of it, and, while he was treating, <hi type="italic">laid his ambushment behind Judah,</hi> against all the laws of arms. What honour could be expected in a <hi type="italic">servant when he reigned?</hi> Abijah was <hi type="italic">for peace,</hi> but, <hi type="italic">when he spoke, they were for war,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.120.7">Ps. cxx. 7</reference>. <div eID="gen8143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8144" type="x-p"/> II. Abijah and his people, who trusted in their God, came off conquerors, notwithstanding the disproportion of their strength and numbers. <div eID="gen8144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8145" type="x-p"/> 1. They were brought into a great strait, put into a great fright, for <hi type="italic">the battle was before and behind.</hi> A good cause, and one which is designed to be victorious, may for a season be involved in embarrassment and distress. It was David's case. <hi type="italic">They compassed me about like bees,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.118.10-Ps.118.12">Ps. cxviii. 10-12</reference>. <div eID="gen8145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8146" type="x-p"/> 2. In their distress, when danger was on every side, which way should they look but upwards for deliverance? It is an unspeakable comfort that no enemy (not the most powerful or politic), no stratagem or ambushment, can cut off our communication with heaven; our way thitherward is always open. (1.) <hi type="italic">They cried unto the Lord,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.14">v. 14</reference>. We hope they did this before they engaged in this war, but the distress they were in made them renew their prayers and quickened them to be importunate. God brings his people into straits, that he may teach them to <hi type="italic">cry unto him.</hi> Earnest praying is crying. (2.) They <hi type="italic">relied on the God of their fathers,</hi> depended upon his power to help them and committed themselves to him, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.18">v. 18</reference>. The prayer of faith is the prevailing prayer, and this is that by which we overcome the world, <hi type="italic">even our faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.5.4">1 John v. 4</reference>. (3.) The <hi type="italic">priests sounded the trumpets</hi> to animate them by giving them an assurance of God's presence with them. It was not only a martial but a sacred sound, and put life into their faith. (4.) They shouted in confidence of victory: "The day is our own, for God is with us." To the cry of the prayer they added the shout of faith, and so became more than conquerors. <div eID="gen8146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8147" type="x-p"/> 3. Thus they obtained a complete victory: <hi type="italic">As the men of Judah shouted</hi> for joy in God's salvation, <hi type="italic">God smote Jeroboam</hi> and his army with such terror and amazement that they could not strike a stroke, but fled with the greatest precipitation imaginable, and the conquerors gave no quarter, so that they put to the sword 500,000 chosen men (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.17">v. 17</reference>), more, it is said, than ever we read of in any history to have been killed in one battle; but the battle was the Lord's, who would thus chastise the idolatry of Israel and own the house of David. But see the sad effect of division: it was the blood of Israelites that was thus shed like water by Israelites, while the heathen, their neighbours, to whom the name of Israel had formerly been a terror, cried, <hi type="italic">Aha!</hi> <hi type="italic">so would we have it.</hi> <div eID="gen8147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8148" type="x-p"/> 4. The consequence of this was that the children of Israel, though they were not brought back to the house of David (which by so great a blow surely they would have been had not the determinate counsel of God been otherwise), yet, for that time, were <hi type="italic">brought under,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.18">v. 18</reference>. Many cities were taken, and remained in the possession of the kings of Judah; as Bethel particularly, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">v. 19</reference>. What became of the golden calf there, when it came into the hands of the king of Judah, we are not told; perhaps it was removed to some place of greater safety, and at length to Samaria (<reference osisRef="Hos.8.5">Hos. viii. 5</reference>); yet in Jehu's time we find it at Bethel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.29">2 Kings x. 29</reference>. Perhaps Abijah, when it was in his power to demolish it, suffered it to stand, for <hi type="italic">his heart was not perfect</hi> with God; and, not improving what he had got for the honour of God, he soon lost it all again. <div eID="gen8148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8149" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> The death of both of the conquered and of the conqueror, not long after. 1. Jeroboam never looked up after this defeat, though he survived it two or three years. He could not recover <hi type="italic">strength again,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.20">v. 20</reference>. The Lord struck him either with some bodily disease, of which he languished, or with melancholy and trouble of mind; his heart was broken, and vexation at his loss brought his head, probably by this time a hoary head, with sorrow to the grave. He escaped the sword of Abijah, but God struck him: and there is no escaping his sword. 2. Abijah waxed mighty upon it. What number of wives and children he had before does not appear; but now he multiplied his wives to fourteen in all, by whom he had thirty-eight children, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.21">v. 21</reference>. Happy is the man that hath his quiver full of those arrows. It seems, he had ways peculiar to himself, and sayings of his own, which were recorded with his acts in the history of those times, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.22">v. 22</reference>. But the number of his months was cut off in the midst, and, soon after his triumphs, death conquered the conqueror. Perhaps he was too much lifted up with his victories, and therefore God would not let him live long to enjoy the honour of them.  <chapter eID="2Chr.13"/> <div eID="gen8149" type="x-p"/>

entries.09e13f0894a29a0b0904976b595c9cea562192b1: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4001"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 13</title> <div sID="gen5781" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.1-2Chr.13.20">2Ch 13:1-20</reference>. Abijah, Succeeding, Makes War against Jeroboam, and Overcomes Him.<div eID="gen5781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5782" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4001"/><hi type="bold">2. His mother's name also was Michaiah, the daughter of Uriel--</hi>the same as Maachah (see on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.2">1Ki 15:2</reference>). She was "the daughter," that is, granddaughter of Absalom (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.2">1Ki 15:2</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Sam.14.1-2Sam.14.33">2Sa 14:1-33</reference>), mother of Abijah, "mother," that is, grandmother (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.10">1Ki 15:10</reference>, Margin) of Asa.<div eID="gen5782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5783" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of Gibeah--</hi>probably implies that Uriel was connected with the house of Saul.<div eID="gen5783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5784" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there was war between Abijah and Jeroboam--</hi>The occasion of this war is not recorded (see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.6">1Ki 15:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.7">7</reference>), but it may be inferred from the tenor of Abijah's address that it arose from his youthful ambition to recover the full hereditary dominion of his ancestors. No prophet now forbade a war with Israel (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.23">2Ch 11:23</reference>) for Jeroboam had forfeited all claim to protection. <div eID="gen5784" type="x-p"/>
entries.8395a7c16eb58a004b6d32e14b70ba9ef5def5b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4002"/><div sID="gen5785" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4002"/><hi type="bold">3. Abijah set the battle in array--</hi>that is, took the field and opened the campaign.<div eID="gen5785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5786" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with ... four hundred thousand chosen men ... Jeroboam with eight hundred thousand--</hi>These are, doubtless, large numbers, considering the smallness of the two kingdoms. It must be borne in mind, however, that Oriental armies are mere mobs--vast numbers accompanying the camp in hope of plunder, so that the gross numbers described as going upon an Asiatic expedition are often far from denoting the exact number of fighting men. But in accounting for the large number of soldiers enlisted in the respective armies of Abijah and Jeroboam, there is no need of resorting to this mode of explanation; for we know by the census of David the immense number of the population that was capable of bearing arms (<reference osisRef="1Chr.21.5">1Ch 21:5</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="2Chr.14.8">2Ch 14:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.17.14">17:14</reference>). <div eID="gen5786" type="x-p"/>
entries.e270a3812dfa8a815c43a6e7b790d5e2f8cb51c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4003"/><div sID="gen5787" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4003"/><hi type="bold">4-12. Abijah stood up upon Mount Zemaraim--</hi>He had entered the enemy's territory and was encamped on an eminence near Beth-el (<reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>). Jeroboam's army lay at the foot of the hill, and as a pitched battle was expected, Abijah, according to the singular usage of ancient times, harangued the enemy. The speakers in such circumstances, while always extolling their own merits, poured out torrents of invective and virulent abuse upon the adversary. So did Abijah. He dwelt on the divine right of the house of David to the throne; and sinking all reference to the heaven-condemned offenses of Solomon and the divine appointment of Jeroboam, as well as the divine sanction of the separation, he upbraided Jeroboam as a usurper, and his subjects as rebels, who took advantage of the youth and inexperience of Rehoboam. Then contrasting the religious state of the two kingdoms, he drew a black picture of the impious innovations and gross idolatry introduced by Jeroboam, with his expulsion and impoverishment (<reference osisRef="2Chr.11.14">2Ch 11:14</reference>) of the Levites. He dwelt with reasonable pride on the pure and regular observance of the ancient institutions of Moses in his own dominion [2Ch 13:11] and concluded with this emphatic appeal: "O children of Israel, fight ye not against Jehovah, the God of your fathers, for ye shall not prosper." <div eID="gen5787" type="x-p"/>
entries.4f4e5b5ca3f5cc78b08dfac890855d9024dcf17c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4004"/><div sID="gen5788" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4004"/><hi type="bold">13-17. But Jeroboam caused an ambushment to come about behind them--</hi>The oration of Abijah, however animating an effect it might have produced on his own troops, was unheeded by the party to whom it was addressed; for while he was wasting time in useless words, Jeroboam had ordered a detachment of his men to move quietly round the base of the hill, so that when Abijah stopped speaking, he and his followers found themselves surprised in the rear, while the main body of the Israelitish forces remained in front. A panic might have ensued, had not the leaders "cried unto the Lord," and the priests "sounded with the trumpets"--the pledge of victory (<reference osisRef="Num.10.9">Nu 10:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Num.31.6">31:6</reference>). Reassured by the well-known signal, the men of Judah responded with a war shout, which, echoed by the whole army, was followed by an impetuous rush against the foe. The shock was resistless. The ranks of the Israelites were broken, for "God smote Jeroboam and all Israel." They took to flight, and the merciless slaughter that ensued can be accounted for only by tracing it to the rancorous passions enkindled by a civil war. <div eID="gen5788" type="x-p"/>
entries.679c5cf5aa33f892c8cfcf96b77f1ab05b5a5e1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4005"/><div sID="gen5789" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4005"/><hi type="bold">19. Abijah pursued after Jeroboam, and took cities from him--</hi>This sanguinary action widened the breach between the people of the two kingdoms. Abijah abandoned his original design of attempting the subjugation of the ten tribes, contenting himself with the recovery of a few border towns, which, though lying within Judah or Benjamin, had been alienated to the new or northern kingdom. Among these was Beth-el, which, with its sacred associations, he might be strongly desirous to wrest from profanation. <div eID="gen5789" type="x-p"/>
entries.11c2d288ba891f0a4245ed4ce6ca35d7759b0df9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv4006"/><div sID="gen5790" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv4006"/><hi type="bold">20. Neither did Jeroboam recover strength again in the days of Abijah--</hi>The disastrous action at Zemaraim, which caused the loss of the flower and chivalry of his army, broke his spirits and crippled his power.<div eID="gen5790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5791" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the Lord struck him, and he died--</hi>that is, Jeroboam. He lived, indeed, two years after the death of Abijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.20">1Ki 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9">15:9</reference>). But he had been threatened with great calamities upon himself and his house, and it is apparently to the execution of these threatenings, which issued in his death, that an anticipatory reference is here made. <chapter eID="2Chr.13"/>

entries.596c1ccc9dd70621ee26505bfb4fc02f7499fa47: <div eID="gen14164" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen14165" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14166" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14166" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen14165" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen14167" type="x-p"/> Abijah begins to reign over Judah, and has war with Jeroboam, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.1-2Chr.13.3">2Chr 13:1-3</reference>. His speech from Mount Zemaraim to Jeroboam, before the commencement of hostilities, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.4-2Chr.13.12">2Chr 13:4-12</reference>. While thus engaged, Jeroboam despatches some troops which come on the rear of Abijah's army, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.13">2Chr 13:13</reference>. Perceiving this, they cry unto the Lord, and the Israelites are defeated with the loss of five hundred thousand men, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.14-2Chr.13.18">2Chr 13:14-18</reference>. Abijah retakes several cities from Jeroboam, who is smitten by the Lord, and dies, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Chr 13:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.20">2Chr 13:20</reference>. Abijah's marriages and issue, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.21">2Chr 13:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.22">2Chr 13:22</reference>.
entries.f686aa95c9c49e0f1d902c3b269b84999ba307af: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen14167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14168" type="x-p"/> His mother's name - was Michaiah - See on <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20">2Chr 11:20</reference> (note).
entries.9e29d6bbefa604676029184bd6b1afff9c3a3c99: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen14168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14169" type="x-p"/> Abijah set the battle in array - The numbers in this verse and in the seventeenth seem almost incredible. Abijah's army consisted of four hundred thousand effective men; that of Jeroboam consisted of eight hundred thousand; and the slain of Jeroboam's army were five hundred thousand. Now it is very possible that there is a cipher too much in all these numbers, and that they should stand thus: Abijah's army, forty thousand; Jeroboam's eighty thousand; the slain, fifty thousand. Calmet, who defends the common reading, allows that the Venice edition of the Vulgate, in 1478; another, in 1489; that of Nuremberg, in 1521; that of Basil, by Froben, in 1538; that of Robert Stevens, in 1546; and many others, have the smaller numbers. Dr. Kennicott says: "On a particular collation of the Vulgate version, it appears that the number of chosen men here slain, which Pope Clement's edition in 1592 determines to be five hundred thousand, the edition of Pope Sixtus, printed two years before, determined to be only fifty thousand; and the two preceding numbers, in the edition of Sixtus, are forty thousand and eighty thousand. As to different printed editions, out of fifty-two, from the year 1462 to 1592, thirty-one contain the less number. And out of fifty-one MSS. twenty-three in the Bodleian library, four in that of Dean Aldrich, and two in that of Exeter College, contain the less number, or else are corrupted irregularly, varying only one or two numbers." <div eID="gen14169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14170" type="x-p"/> This examination was made by Dr. Kennicott before he had finished his collation of Hebrew MSS., and before De Rossi had published his Variae Lectiones Veteris Testamenti; but from these works we find little help, as far as the Hebrew MSS. are concerned. One Hebrew MS., instead of ארבע מאות אלף arba meoth eleph, four hundred thousand, reads ארבע עשר אלף arba eser eleph, fourteen thousand. <div eID="gen14170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14171" type="x-p"/> In all printed copies of the Hebrew, the numbers are as in the common text, four hundred thousand, eight hundred thousand, and five hundred thousand. <div eID="gen14171" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> The versions are as follow: - The Targum, or Chaldee, the same in each place as the Hebrew. <div eID="gen14172" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14173" type="x-p"/> The Syriac in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">2Chr 13:3</reference> has four hundred thousand young men for the army of Abijah, and eight hundred thousand stout youth for that of Jeroboam. For the slain Israelites, in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.17">2Chr 13:17</reference>, it has five hundred thousand, falsely translated in the Latin text quinque milia, five thousand, both in the Paris and London Polyglots: another proof among many that little dependence is to be placed on the Latin translation of this version in either of the above Polyglots. <div eID="gen14173" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14174" type="x-p"/> The Arabic is the same in all these cases with the Syriac, from which it has been translated. <div eID="gen14174" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14175" type="x-p"/> The Septuagint, both as it is published in all the Polyglots, and as far as I have seen in MSS. is the same with the Hebrew text. So also is Josephus. <div eID="gen14175" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14176" type="x-p"/> The Vulgate or Latin version is that alone that exhibits any important variations; we have had considerable proof of this in the above-mentioned collations of Calmet and Kennicott. I shall beg liberty to add others from my own collection. <div eID="gen14176" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14177" type="x-p"/> In the Editio Princeps of the Latin Bible, though without date or place, yet evidently printed long before that of Fust, in 1462, the places stand thus: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">2Chr 13:3</reference>. Cumque inisset certamen, et haberet bellicosissimos viros, et electorum Quadraginta milia: Iheroboam construxit e contra aciem Octoginta milia virorum; "With him Abia entered into battle; and he had of the most warlike and choice men forty thousand; and Jeroboam raised an army against him of eighty thousand men." And in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.17">2Chr 13:17</reference> : Et corruerunt vulnerati ex Israel, Quinquaginta milia virorum fortium; "And there fell down wounded fifty thousand stout men of Israel." In the Glossa Ordinaria, by Strabo Fuldensis, we have forty thousand and eighty thousand in the two first instances, and five hundred thousand in the last. - Bib. Sacr. vol. ii., Antv. 1634. <div eID="gen14177" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14178" type="x-p"/> In six ancient MSS. of my own, marked A, B, C, D, E, F. the text stands thus: - <div eID="gen14178" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14179" type="x-p"/> A. - Cumque inisset Abia certamen, et haberet bellicosissimos viros, et electorum XL. MIL. Jeroboam instruxit contra aciem LXXX. MIL. <div eID="gen14179" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> And in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.17">2Chr 13:17</reference> : Et corruerunt vulnerati ex Israel L. MIL. virorum fortium. Here we have forty thousand for the army of Abijah, and eighty thousand for that of Jeroboam, and Fifty thousand for the slain of the latter. <div eID="gen14180" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14181" type="x-p"/> B. - <div eID="gen14181" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14182" type="x-p"/> Quadraginita milia Forty thousand Octoginta milia Eighty thousand Quinquiaginta milia Fifty thousand <div eID="gen14182" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14183" type="x-p"/> The numbers being here expressed in words at full length, there can be no suspicion of mistake. <div eID="gen14183" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14184" type="x-p"/> C. - <div eID="gen14184" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14185" type="x-p"/> CCCC milia 400 thousand DCCC milibus 800 thousand D milia 500 thousand <div eID="gen14185" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14186" type="x-p"/> This is the same as the Hebrew text, and very distinctly expressed. <div eID="gen14186" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> D. - xl. m. 40,000 lxxx. m. 80,000 l. v. m. 50 and 5000 <div eID="gen14187" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> This, in the two first numbers, is the same as the others above; but the last is confused, and appears to stand for fifty thousand and five thousand. A later hand has corrected the two first cccc numbers in this MS., placing over the first four CCCC, thus 40, thus changing forty into four hundred; and over the second thus, dccc lxxx., thus changing eighty into eight hundred. Over the latter number, which is evidently a mistake of the scribe, there is no correction. <div eID="gen14188" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> E. - xl. m. 40,000 Octoginta m. Eighty thousand l. m. 50,000 <div eID="gen14189" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14190" type="x-p"/> F. - <div eID="gen14190" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> CCCC. m. 400,000 DCCC. m. 800,000 D. m. 600,000 <div eID="gen14191" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> This also is the same as the Hebrew. <div eID="gen14192" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> The reader has now the whole evidence which I have been able to collect before him, and may choose; the smaller numbers appear to be the most correct. Corruptions in the numbers in these historical books we have often had cause to suspect, and to complain of.
entries.346d69d6d9b97d42fa5844a41a1ccf2a4726501e: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen14193" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> Stood up upon Mount Zemaraim - "Which was a mount of the tribe of the house of Ephraim." - Targum. Jarchi thinks that Abijah went to the confines of the tribe of Ephraim to attack Jeroboam. It could not be Shomeron, the mount on which Samaria was built in the days of Omri king of Israel, <reference osisRef="1Kgs.16.24">1Kgs 16:24</reference>.
entries.4c04d8d38fe6e93546b5e458efc67d8ac5ed42c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen14194" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> By a covenant of salt? - For ever. "For as the waters of the sea never grow sweet, neither shall the dominion depart from the house of David." - Targum. See my note on <reference osisRef="Num.18.19">Num 18:19</reference> (note).
entries.3ed907b56dd9420d7db8baeff944611d072ec7c0: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen14195" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> When Rehoboam was young and tender-hearted - Therefore he could not be forty-one when he came to the throne; see the note on <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">2Chr 13:3</reference>. Children of Belial here signifies men of the most abandoned principles and characters; or men without consideration, education, or brains.
entries.d4153f25086cf391a59a575543510478c7cc7c92: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen14196" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> A young bullock and seven rams - He who could provide these for his own consecration was received into the order of this spurious and wicked priesthood. Some think he who could give to Jeroboam a young bullock and seven rams, was thereby received into the priesthood; this being the price for which the priesthood was conferred. The former is most likely.
entries.c92244e07559696ef080eb38c432ee574c329177: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen14197" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> The Lord is our God - We have not abandoned the Lord; and we still serve him according to his own law.
entries.7762800d53b2551574002e9267c4c5c357c97dfb: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen14198" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> God himself is with us - Ye have golden calves; we have the living and omnipotent Jehovah. <div eID="gen14199" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14200" type="x-p"/> With - trumpets to cry alarm against you - This was appalling: When the priests sound their trumpets, it will be a proof that the vengeance of the Lord shall speedily descend upon you.
entries.9d9bda5f7834fc699a0b4cc116c36017def5ab57: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen14200" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> But Jeroboam caused an ambushment - While Abijah was thus employed in reproving them, Jeroboam divided his army privately, and sent a part to take Abijah in the rear; and this must have proved fatal to the Jews, had not the Lord interposed.
entries.7f9ce7b994deeda56b697b6fb72f5edea0f60183: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen14201" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> Slain - five hundred thousand chosen men - Query, fifty thousand? This was a great slaughter: see the note on <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">2Chr 13:3</reference>, where all these numbers are supposed to be overcharged.
entries.05155e769b69918fec91bb345c1cda8069442940: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen14202" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14203" type="x-p"/> Judah prevailed, because - "They depended on the Word of the God of their fathers." - T.
entries.cbcc6cac0b69b98f828c52641839b3ad5eea8a90: <hi type="bold">Verse 19</hi> <div eID="gen14203" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> Beth-el - "Beth-lehem." - Targum. <div eID="gen14204" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> Jeshanah - We know not where these towns lay.
entries.13c7cd46c14014a9c72e2dba6a5669ebc1ce947f: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen14205" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14206" type="x-p"/> The Lord struck him, and he died - Who died? Abijah or Jeroboam? Some think it was Jeroboam; some, that it was Abijah. Both rabbins and Christians are divided on this point; nor is it yet settled. The prevailing opinion is that Jeroboam is meant, who was struck then with that disease of which he died about two years after; for he did not die till two years after Abijah: see <reference osisRef="1Kgs.14.20">1Kgs 14:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.9">1Kgs 15:9</reference>. It seems as if Jeroboam was meant, not Abijah.
entries.e542dcf8932c195bfa68f8c55e04f286c0424cb1: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen14206" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> Married fourteen wives - Probably he made alliances with the neighboring powers, by taking their daughters to him for wives.
entries.c0fb724dc59019873b01aa1fd554532fefccd1da: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen14207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> Written in the story - במדרש bemidrash, "in the commentary;" this, as far as I recollect, is the first place where a midrash or commentary is mentioned. The margin is right. <div eID="gen14208" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen14209" type="x-p"/> His ways, and his sayings - The commentary of the prophet Iddo is lost. What his sayings were we cannot tell; but from the specimen in this chapter, he appears to have been a very able speaker, and one who knew well how to make the best use of his argument.  <chapter eID="2Chr.13"/> <div eID="gen14209" type="x-p"/>

entries.98413cad9b31504ecfbedd59ac3a665b40942685: <div eID="gen5997" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s2">The Reign of Abijah - 2 Chronicles 13</title> <div sID="gen5998" type="x-p"/> In the book of Kings it is merely remarked in general, that the hostile relationship between Jeroboam and Rehoboam continued during his whole life, and that between Abijah and Jeroboam there was war (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.6">2Ch 13:6</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.7">2Ch 13:7</reference>); but not one of his enterprises is recounted, and only his attitude towards the Lord is exactly characterized. In our chapter, on the contrary, we have a vivid and circumstantial narrative of the commencement, course, and results of a great war against Jeroboam, in which Abijah, with the help of the Lord, inflicted a crushing defeat on the great army of the Israelites, and conquered several cities. <div eID="gen5998" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5999" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.1-2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:1-2</reference> <div eID="gen5999" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6000" type="x-p"/> The commencement and duration of the reign, as in 1Ki 15:1-2. Abijah’s mother is here (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.2">2Ch 13:2</reference>) called Michaiah instead of Maachah, as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20">2Ch 11:20</reference> and 1Ki 15:2, but it can hardly be a second name which Maachah had received for some unknown reason; probably מיכיהו is a mere orthographical error for מעכה. She is here called, not the daughter = granddaughter of Abishalom, but after her father, the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah; see on 2Ch 11:20.<note placement="foot">Against this Bertheau remarks, after the example of Thenius: “When we consider that the wife of Abijah and mother of Asa was also called Maachah, 1Ki 15:13; <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2Ch 15:16</reference>, and that in 1Ki 15:2 this Maachah is again called the daughter of Abishalom, and that this latter statement is not met with in the Chronicle, we are led to conjecture that Maachah, the mother of Abijah, the daughter of Abishalom, has been confounded with Maachah the mother of Asa, the daughter of Uriel of Gibeah, and that in our passage Asa’s mother is erroneously named instead of the mother of Abijah.” This conjecture is a strange fabric of perverted facts and inconsequential reasoning. In 1Ki 15:2 Abijam’s mother is called Maachah the daughter of Abishalom, exactly as in <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.20">2Ch 11:20</reference> and <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:21</reference>; and in 1Ki 15:13, in perfect agreement with <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2Ch 15:16</reference>, it is stated that Asa removed Maachah from the dignity of Gebira because she had made herself a statute of Asherah. This Maachah, deposed by Asa, is called in 1Ki 15:10 the daughter of Abishalom, and only this latter remark is omitted from the Chronicle. How from these statements we must conclude that the mother of Abijah, Maachah the daughter of Abishalom, has been confounded with Maachah the mother of Asa, the daughter of Uriel, we cannot see. The author of the book of Kings knows only one Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom, whom in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.2">2Ch 15:2</reference> he calls mother, i.e., גּבירה, i.e., Sultana Walide of Abijah, and in <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.10">2Ch 15:10</reference> makes to stand in the same relationship of mother to Asa. From this, however, the only natural and logically sound conclusion which can be drawn is that Abijam’s mother, Rehoboam’s wife, occupied the position of queen-mother, not merely during the three years’ reign of Abijam, but also during the first years of the reign of his son Asa, as his grandmother, until Asa had deprived her of this dignity because of her idolatry. It is nowhere said in Scripture that this woman was Abijam’s wife, but that is a conclusion drawn by Thenius and Bertheau only from her being called אמּו, his (Asa’s) mother, as if אם could denote merely the actual mother, and not the grandmother. Finally, the omission in the Chronicle of the statement in 1Ki 15:10, “The name of his mother was Maachah, the daughter of Abishalom,” does not favour in the very least the conjecture that Asa’s mother has been confounded with the mother of Abijah; for it is easily explained by the fact that at the accession of Asa no change was made in reference to the dignity of queen-mother, Abijah’s mother still holding that position even under Asa.</note><hi type="italic">The War between Abijah and Jeroboam</hi>. - היתה מלחמה, war arose, broke out.
entries.3747fa0ca0b7195b4f3817eaa9baaefc33753e10: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.3">2Ch 13:3</reference> <div eID="gen6000" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6001" type="x-p"/> Abijah began the war with an army of 400,000 valiant warriors. בּחוּר אישׁ, chosen men. את מ אסר, to bind on war, i.e., to open the war. Jeroboam prepared for the war with 800,000 warriors. The number of Jeroboam’s warriors is exactly that which Joab returned as the result, as to Israel, of the numbering of the people commanded by David, while that of Abijah’s army is less by 100,000 men than Joab numbered in Judah (<reference osisRef="2Sam.24.9">2Sa 24:9</reference>).
entries.b1d8a5f2cb268c3bd4399033c7d76ba1ea76391c: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.4">2Ch 13:4</reference> <div eID="gen6001" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6002" type="x-p"/> When the two armies lay over against each other, ready for the combat, Abijah addressed the enemy, King Jeroboam and all Israel, in a speech from Mount Zemaraim. The mountain צמרים is met with only here; but a city of this name is mentioned in <reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>, whence we would incline to the conclusion that the mountain near or upon which this city lay was intended. But if this city was situated to the east, not only of Bethel, but also of Jerusalem, on the road to Jericho (see on <reference osisRef="Josh.18.22">Jos 18:22</reference>), as we may conclude from its enumeration between Beth-arabah and Bethel in Josh. <hi type="italic">loc. cit.</hi>, it will not suit our passage, at least if Zemaraim be really represented by the ruin el Sumra to the east of Khan Hadur on the way from Jerusalem to Jericho. Robinson (<hi type="italic">Phys. Geog.</hi> S. 38) conjectures Mount Zemaraim to the east of Bethel, near the border of the two kingdoms, to which Mount Ephraim also extends. Abijah represented first of all (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.5-2Chr.13.7">2Ch 13:5-7</reference>) to Jeroboam and the Israelites that their kingdom was the result of a revolt against Jahve, who had given the kingship over Israel to David and his sons for ever.
entries.2f0b38caf0c9b9aaae884d7e554bc19e2ae39f51: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.5-2Chr.13.7">2Ch 13:5-7</reference> “Is it not to you to know?” i.e., can it be unknown to you? מלח בּרית, accus. of nearer definition: after the fashion of a covenant of salt, i.e., of an irrevocable covenant; cf. on <reference osisRef="Lev.2.13">Lev 2:13</reference> and Num 18:19. “And Jeroboam, the servant of Solomon the son of David (cf. 1Ki 11:11), rebelled against his lord,” with the help of frivolous, worthless men (רקים as in Jdg 9:4; Jdg 11:3; בליּעל בּני as in 1Ki 21:10, 1Ki 21:13 -not recurring elsewhere in the Chronicle), who gathered around him, and rose against Rehoboam with power. על התאמּץ, to show oneself powerful, to show power against any one. Against this rising Rehoboam showed himself not strong enough, because he was an inexperienced man and soft of heart. נער denotes not “a boy,” for Rehoboam was forty-one years old when he entered upon his reign, but “an inexperienced young man,” as in 1Ch 29:1. לבב רך, soft of heart, i.e., faint-hearted, inclined to give way, without energy to make a stand against those rising insolently against him. lp' התחזק ולא, and showed himself not strong before them, proved to be too weak in opposition to them. This representation does not conform to the state of the case as narrated in 2 Chron 10. Rehoboam did not appear soft-hearted and compliant in the negotiation with the rebellious tribes at Sichem; on the contrary, he was hard and defiant, and showed himself youthfully inconsiderate only in throwing to the winds the wise advice of the older men, and in pursuance of the rash counsel of the young men who had grown up with him, brought about the rupture by his domineering manner. But Abijah wishes to justify his father as much as possible in his speech, and shifts all the guilt of the rebellion of the ten tribes from the house of David on to Jeroboam and his worthless following.
entries.899125ce0f543790e96250e96637ecccbf650ed6: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.8-2Chr.13.9">2Ch 13:8-9</reference> <div eID="gen6002" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6003" type="x-p"/> Abijah then points out to his opponents the vanity of their trust in the great multitude of their warriors and their gods, while yet they had driven out the priests of Jahve. “And now ye say,” <hi type="italic">scil.</hi> in your heart, i.e., you think to show yourself strong before the kingdom of Jahve in the hands of the sons of David, i.e., against the kingdom of Jahve ruled over by the sons of David, by raising a great army in order to make war upon and to destroy this kingdom. רב המון ואתּם, and truly ye are a great multitude, and with you are the golden calves, which Jeroboam hath made to you for gods; but trust not unto them, for Jahve, the true God, have ye not for you as a helper.
entries.1bbefa9504d7627e61a8a5c4b127a93a188c8a1f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.10-2Chr.13.11">2Ch 13:10-11</reference> <div eID="gen6003" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6004" type="x-p"/> While, therefore, the Israelites have no-gods in their golden calves, Judah has Jahve for its God, whom it worships in His temple in the manner prescribed by Moses. “But in Jahve is our God, and we have not forsaken Him,” in so far, viz., as they observed the legal Jahve-worship. So Abijah himself explains his words, “as priests serve Him the sons of Aaron (who were chosen by Jahve), and the Levites are בּמלאכת, in service,” i.e., performing the service prescribed to them. As essential parts of that service of God, the offering of the daily burnt-offering and the daily incense-offering (Exo 29:38., <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.7">2Ch 30:7</reference>), the laying out of the shew-bread (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.30">Exo 25:30</reference>; Lev 24:5.), the lighting of the lamps of the golden candlesticks (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.37">Exo 25:37</reference>; Exo 27:20.), are mentioned. In this respect they keep the יהוה משׁמרת (cf. <reference osisRef="Lev.8.35">Lev 8:35</reference>).
entries.0c23517bcbb844f970cf34ee0477df858858f7cf: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.12">2Ch 13:12</reference> <div eID="gen6004" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6005" type="x-p"/> Abijah draws from all this the conclusion: “Behold, with us at our head are (not the two calves of gold, but) God (האלהים with the article, the true God) and His priests, and the alarm-trumpets to sound against you.” He mentions the trumpets as being the divinely appointed pledges that God would remember them in war, and would deliver them from their enemies, Num 10:9. Then he closes with a warning to the Israelites not to strive with Jahve, the God of their fathers.
entries.efc482fa5c3107ecdaf3ab516a3718471193a50f: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.13-2Chr.13.15">2Ch 13:13-15</reference> <div eID="gen6005" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6006" type="x-p"/> The war; Judah’s victory, and the defeat of Jeroboam and the Israelites. - 2Ch 13:13. Jeroboam caused the ambush (the troops appointed to be an ambush) to go round about, so as to come upon their rear (i.e., of the men of Judah); and so they (the main division of Jeroboam’s troops) were before Judah, and the ambush in their rear (i.e., of the men of Judah); and the men of Judah, when they turned themselves (<hi type="italic">scil.</hi> to attack), saw war before and behind them, i.e., perceived that they were attacked in front and rear. In this dangerous position the men of Judah cried to the Lord, and the priests blew the trumpets (<reference osisRef="2Chr.13.15">2Ch 13:15</reference>); and as they raised this war-cry, God smote their enemies so that they took to flight. In ויּריעוּ and בּהריע the loud shout of the warriors and the clangour of the trumpets in the hands of the priests are comprehended; and הריע is neither to be taken to refer only to the war-cry raised by the warriors in making the attack, nor, with Bertheau, to be referred only to the blowing of the trumpets.
entries.dbae0897d46283c5377f03678871f78ec0d16f33: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.16-2Chr.13.17">2Ch 13:16-17</reference> <div eID="gen6006" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6007" type="x-p"/> So Abijah and his people inflicted a great blow (defeat) on the Israelites, so that 500,000 of them, i.e., more than the half of Jeroboam’s whole army, fell.
entries.2a4ae3d5507ed614746249edbe22c0ea20511e69: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.18-2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:18-19</reference> <div eID="gen6007" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6008" type="x-p"/> The results of this victory. The Israelites were bowed down, their power weakened; the men of Judah became strong, mighty, because they relied upon Jahve their God. Following up his victory, Abijah took from Jeroboam several cities with their surrounding domains: Bethel, the present Beitin, see on <reference osisRef="Josh.7.2">Jos 7:2</reference>; Jeshanah, occurring only here, and the position of which has not yet been ascertained; and Ephron (עפרון, Keth.; the <hi type="italic">Keri</hi>, on the contrary, עפרין). This city cannot well be identified with Mount Ephron, <reference osisRef="Josh.15.9">Jos 15:9</reference>; for that mountain was situated on the southern frontier of Benjamin, not far from Jerusalem, while the city Ephron is to be sought much farther north, in the neighbourhood of Bethel. C. v. Raumer and others identify Ephron or Ephrain both with Ophrah of Benjamin, which, it is conjectured, was situated near or in Tayibeh, to the east of Bethel, and with the Ἐφραΐ́μ, Joh 11:54, whither Jesus withdrew into the wilderness, which, according to Josephus, <hi type="italic">Bell. Jud</hi>. iv. 9. 9, lay in the neighbourhood of Bethel. See on Jos 18:23.<note placement="foot">The account of this war, which is peculiar to the Chronicle, and which de Wette declared, on utterly insufficient grounds, to be an invention of the chronicler (cf. against him my apol. <hi type="italic">Vers. über die Chron.</hi> S. 444ff.), is thus regarded by Ewald (<hi type="italic">Gesch. Isr.</hi> iii. S. 466, der 2 Aufl.): “The chronicler must certainly have found among his ancient authorities an account of this conclusion of the war, and we cannot but believe that we have here, in so far, authentic tradition;” and only the details of the description are the results of free expansion by the chronicler, but in the speech <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.4-2Chr.13.13">2Ch 13:4-13</reference> every word and every thought is marked by the peculiar colouring of the Chronicle. But this last assertion is contradicted by Ewald’s own remark, i. S. 203, that “in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.4-2Chr.13.7">2Ch 13:4-7</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19-2Chr.13.21">2Ch 13:19-21</reference>, an antiquated manner of speech and representation appears, while in the other verses, on the contrary, those usual with the chronicler are found,” - in support of which he adduces the words בליּעל בּני, <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.7">2Ch 13:7</reference>, and מלח בּרית, 2Ch 13:5. According to this view, Abijah’s speech cannot have been freely draughted by the chronicler, but must have been derived, at least so far as the fundamental thoughts are concerned, from an ancient authority, doubtless the Midrash of the prophet Iddo, cited in 2Ch 13:22. But Ewald’s further remark (iii. S. 466), that the author of the Chronicle, because he regarded the heathenized Samaria of his time as the true representative of the old kingdom of the ten tribes, seized this opportunity to put into King Abijah’s mouth a long denunciatory and didactic speech, addressed at the commencement of the battle to the enemy as rebels not merely against the house of David, but also against the true religion, is founded upon the unscriptural idea that the calf-worship of the Israelites was merely a somewhat sensuous form of the true Jahve-worship, and was fundamentally distinct from the heathen idolatry, and also from the idolatry of the later Samaritans. In the judgment of all the prophets, not only of Hosea and Amos, but also of the prophetic author of the book of Kings, the calf-worship was a defection from Jahve, the God of the fathers, - a forsaking of the commands of Jahve, and a serving of the Baals; cf. e.g., 1 Kings 13; 2 Kings 17:7-23. What Abijah says of the calf-worship of the Israelites, and of Judah’s attitude to Jahve and His worship in the temple, is founded on the truth, and is also reconcilable with the statement in 1Ki 15:3, that Abijah’s heart was not wholly devoted to the Lord, like David’s heart. Abijah had promoted the legal temple-worship even by consecratory gifts (1Ki 15:15), and could consequently quite well bring forward the worship of God in Judah as the true worship, in contrast to the Israelitic calf-worship, for the discouragement of his enemies, and for the encouragement of his own army; and we may consequently regard the kernel, or the essential contents of the speech, as being historically well-founded. The account of the war, moreover, is also shown to be historical by the exact statement as to the conquered cities in <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.19">2Ch 13:19</reference>, which evidently has been derived from ancient authorities. Only in the statements about the number of warriors, and of the slain Israelites, the numbers are not to be estimated according to the literal value of the figures; for they are, as has been already hinted in the commentary, only an expression in figures of the opinion of contemporaries of the war, that both kings had made a levy of all the men in their respective kingdoms capable of bearing arms, and that Jeroboam was defeated with such slaughter that he lost more than the half of his warriors.</note>
entries.1f82f5285fe809568d275f7ee3ecb4c67b43d765: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.20">2Ch 13:20</reference> <div eID="gen6008" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6009" type="x-p"/> Jeroboam could not afterwards gain power (כּוח עצר, as in <reference osisRef="1Chr.29.14">1Ch 29:14</reference>): “And Jahve smote him, and he died.” The meaning of this remark is not clear, since we know nothing further of the end of Jeroboam’s life than that he died two years after Abijah. ויּגּפהוּ can hardly refer to the unfortunate result of the war (2Ch 13:15.), for Jeroboam outlived the war by several years. We would be more inclined to understand it of the blow mentioned in 1Ki 14:1-8, when God announced to him by Ahijah the extermination of his house, and took away his son Abijah, who was mourned by all Israel.
entries.515ced53d2a367e17d29e61cd4429b89eb276f88: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.21">2Ch 13:21</reference> <hi type="italic">Wives and children of Abijah. His death</hi>. - 2Ch 13:21. While Jeroboam was not able to recover from the defeat he had suffered, Abijah established himself in his kingdom (יתחזּק, cf. <reference osisRef="2Chr.12.13">2Ch 12:13</reference>), and took to himself fourteen wives. The taking of these wives is not to be regarded as later in time than his establishment of his rule after the victory over Jeroboam. Since Abijah reigned only three years, he must have already had the greater number of his wives and children when he ascended the throne, as we may gather also from <reference osisRef="2Chr.11.21">2Ch 11:21</reference>-23. The ו consec. with ישּׂא serves only to connect logically the information as to his wives and children with the preceding, as the great increase of his family was a sign of Abijah’s increase in strength, while Jeroboam’s dynasty was soon extirpated.
entries.8bf714ae0453108904c6cf365a5b501fcf962c22: <reference osisRef="2Chr.13.22">2Ch 13:22</reference> <div eID="gen6009" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen6010" type="x-p"/> As to the מדרשׁ of the prophet Iddo, see the Introduction. 13:23 (<hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="2Chr.14.1">2Ch 14:1</reference></hi>). This is remarked here, because this rest was also a result of Abijah’s great victory over Jeroboam.  <chapter eID="2Chr.13"/> <div eID="gen6010" type="x-p"/>
